The structure is described in the body-centered tetragonal space group I4/m (number 87, Hall symbol –I 4), but the atomic positions are supplied in a nonstandard input cell rather than the conventional tetragonal cell. The input lattice has all three edge lengths equal to 5.77457662 Å, with interaxial angles α = 122.8014197°, β = 122.8014197°, and γ = 85.21263594000001°. This ten-atom input cell contains two Sr, one Mn, one Sb, and six O atoms. Fractional coordinates in the input frame, q_input, are related to those in the standard I4/m frame, q_standard, by q_standard = P q_input + s, where the origin shift s is (0, 0, 0) and the transformation matrix P has rows (0.5, −0.5, 0.5000000000000001), (0.49999999999999994, −0.4999999999999998, −0.5), and (0.49999999999999994, 0.5, −0.5). Coordinate values were rounded to six decimal places, and no additional positional corrections were required.

In the standard frame, the ten-atom input contents expand under the body-centered tetragonal symmetry into five independent crystallographic orbits. Strontium occupies the fourfold Wyckoff site 4d, whose representative position is (0, 1/2, 1/4); the four symmetry-equivalent Sr atoms are generated from this fixed coordinate triplet with no free positional parameters. Manganese lies on the twofold site 2b at (0, 0, 1/2), while antimony occupies the twofold site 2a at the origin (0, 0, 0); both positions are likewise fully fixed by symmetry.

Oxygen is distributed over two inequivalent sublattices. The first oxygen orbit is the fourfold site 4e, described by the coordinate relation (0, 0, z) with the single free parameter z = 0.23350400000000002, so its representative atom sits on the fourfold axis slightly below one-quarter of the standard-cell c repeat. The second oxygen orbit is the eightfold site 8h, described by (x, y, 0) with x = 0.20449299999999992 and y = 0.6964279999999999; these atoms lie in the z = 0 plane, with the eight equivalent positions generated by the I4/m symmetry operations. Together, the fixed Sr, Mn, and Sb sites and the two oxygen orbits—one axial with variable z and one basal-plane orbit with independent x and y—define the complete atomic geometry when mapped back to the stated input cell through the inverse of the supplied frame transformation.
